deals.headline: Morningstar founder Joe Mansueto buys 49% of the Chicago Fire
deals.summary: Mansueto bought a 49% stake from Andrew Hauptman, who stayed chairman and controlling shareholder; Mansueto became vice chairman and alternate governor. The club did not release terms; Forbes later reported the stake was bought at a $240 million valuation. Advisers: Moelis and Latham & Watkins for Andell, BDT & Company and Covington & Burling for Mansueto Sports, LLC.

deals.evidence: The Chicago Fire will pay $65.5 million to leave the suburban Chicago stadium
deals.headline: Fire pay $65.5 million to leave the Bridgeview stadium lease
deals.summary: Agreement with the Village of Bridgeview to end the lease at SeatGeek Stadium (originally to 2036): $10 million upfront, $5 million for upgrades to soccer facilities near the stadium, and the $50.5 million balance through 2036. The first team moved to Soldier Field from 2020; training and the academy stayed in Bridgeview at the time.

deals.headline: Mansueto buys Hauptman's controlling 51% and becomes sole owner
deals.summary: Hauptman sold his controlling interest and Mansueto became chairman and sole owner. The club did not disclose terms; Forbes reported, citing multiple sources, that Mansueto paid $204 million for the 51% he did not own, valuing the club at $400 million.

deals.date_text: Stadium plan announced June 2025; groundbreaking 3 March 2026
deals.evidence: officially broke ground on its new $750 million privately-funded soccer stadium in the South Loop
deals.headline: Fire break ground on $750 million privately funded stadium at The 78
deals.summary: Privately funded, open-air stadium for more than 22,000 at The 78 on the Chicago River (Related Midwest master developer, Gensler architect), due to open ahead of the 2028 MLS season. The club says Mansueto has committed more than $1 billion to the club since taking full ownership in 2019, including the $100 million Endeavor Health Performance Center.

notes: US clubs publish no accounts: revenue and operating income are Forbes estimates for the 2025 season (operating income is EBITDA as Forbes defines it; playoffs, transfers and shared MLS distributions excluded). Forbes figures, and Soldier Field's own about page, are cited from Wayback Machine copies because forbes.com and soldierfield.com refuse automated fetches (HTTP 403/406); the live URLs are in sources. Stadium capacity is Soldier Field's full capacity as its operator states it; the earlier record's 24,955 (from Wikipedia) looks like the reduced configuration used for Fire matches, but no citable page states it, so it was not kept. Owner stake of 100% rests on the club's own words 'full ownership' (and 'sole owner' in its September 2019 release; the Chicago Tribune reported Hauptman sold his 51%). No minority, institutional or private-equity investor is named anywhere. Not found: legal entity and registry, average attendance, wages, social follower counts with a stated date.
